newsitem.title: UK: Full text of September 4 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of September 4 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: The following is the complete text of the minutes of the September 4 monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George.
MONETARY AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS

2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by officials before the meeting) provided further evidence that cost and price pressures remained weak. While output growth remained below trend, more forward-looking indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were more buoyant.
Inflation Indicators
3. Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest payments - RPIX) was unchanged in July, at 2.8 per cent. All-items RPI inflation rose by 0.1 percentage point, to 2.2 percent.
4. Most other price and cost indicators confirmed that inflationary pressures remained weak:
-- sterling non-oil commodity prices fell by 0.6 per cent in July. However, the oil price had risen significantly to $21.9 per barrel, reflecting increased tensions in the Middle East;
-- sterling's effective exchange rate index rose by 0.7 over the period since the last meeting, to stand at 85.8;

-- total non-oil import prices rose by 0.8 per cent in the three months to June compared to the previous three months, but were just 1 per cent higher than a year ago. Non-EC import prices fell by 0.7 per cent in the three months to July, and the annual rate fell from 1.1 per cent to 0.4 per cent;

-- producer input prices for manufacturing (excluding food, beverage, tobacco and petroleum industries) fell in July, by 0.8 per cent; and compared to a year ago they were 6.7 per cent lower. The CIPS survey input price indicator rose in August, but remained low;

-- producer output prices (excluding FBTP) also fell, by 0.1 per cent in July; and the annual inflation rate fell to 1.5 per cent, from 2.0 per cent in June. The CBI survey output price expectations balance increased slightly in August, but remained at a low level;
-- the annual growth rate of underlying average earnings was unchanged in June, at 3.75 percent. IRS median pay settlements were unchanged at 3.0 per cent in July.
MONETARY AND FINANCIAL INDICATORS
5. Notes and coin grew by 0.8 per cent in August, up from 0.6 per cent in July and the annual growth rate rose to 7.5 percent, from 7.1 percent in July.

6. M4 grew by 0.5 percent in July, down from 0.6 percent in June; and the annual growth rate fell to 9.0 percent, down from 9.9 percent in June. Growth in M4 lending was unchanged in July, at 0.7 percent.

7. The Halifax house price index rose by 0.4 percent in August, following a rise of 0.5 percent in July; the index was up 5.8 percent on a year earlier. The Nationwide index rose by 1.8 percent in August, leaving the index 5.5 percent up on a year earlier. Housing market transactions continued to recover; particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) in the three months to July were 7.3 percent up on the previous three months, and 5.0 percent up on a year earlier.

8. Short-term interest rates were around 8 basis points higher in the US since the last meeting, but had fallen by around 20 basis points in Japan and in Germany (reflecting the cut in the Bundesbank's repo rate). Official rates had been reduced in a number of other European countries, including France and the Netherlands. UK short-term interest rates were little changed from last month; and forward interest rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts were also little changed for September 1996, but had fallen (by up to 15 basis points) for longer maturities.

9. 10-year bond yields in the US had risen by around 7 basis points, but had fallen by nearly 30 basis points in Japan, and were little changed in Germany. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts were little changed at all maturities. Since the last meeting inflation expectations implied by the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) had fallen slightly (by around 5 basis points) for five years ahead, but had risen by around 10 basis points for ten years ahead.
ACTIVITY INDICATORS
10. Overseas data indicated that US activity remained strong, and there were signs of recovery in Germany. Indicators in Japan were mixed:
-- US industrial production rose by 0.2 per cent in July, following a rise of 0.6 per cent in June. GDP was provisionally estimated to have grown in 1996 Q2 by 1.2percent;
-- in Germany industrial production rose by 0.2 percent in July, following a rise of 0.7 percent in June;
-- in Japan industrial production rose by 4.1 percent in July, following a fall of 4.3 percent in June, but the Tankan survey of business confidence was weak.

11. The latest estimate of UK GDP growth in Q2 was unchanged at 0.4 percent, leaving it 1.8 percent up on a year earlier. Other activity data were also consistent with growth overall continuing below trend, but indicators of business confidence and consumer demand remained stronger:

-- manufacturing output fell by 0.3 percent in June. However, in the three months to June it was unchanged on a year earlier. Total industrial output fell by 1.1 percent in June, but in the latest three months was up 1.1 percent on a year earlier;
-- all major business surveys were more buoyant. The August CIPS and CBI surveys both showed an increase in output and new orders' indicators;
-- retail sales fell by 0.6 percent in July, following a rise of 1.5 percent in June. However, in the three months to July sales were 2.7 percent higher than in the same period a year earlier;

-- survey indicators in the retail sector remained strong: consumer confidence rose slightly, and in the July CBI Distributive Trades Survey the balance of retailers expecting higher sales remained at a high level by historical standards;
-- claimant unemployment fell by 24,100 in July, to its lowest level since March 1991, and unfilled vacancies at Jobcentres increased by 11,500.
SUMMARY OF DISCUSSION

12. The Governor said that the economic and monetary data that had become available over the holiday period did not alter the overall picture discussed at the last meeting. The short-term outlook for inflation remained favourable. Underlying domestic demand continued to trend upwards, and there was growing evidence in the surveys that this was beginning to feed through into output - as would be expected as the downward stock adjustment worked itself through. The monetary data - and the direct economic forecasts - were still consistent with these trends in demand and output continuing into next year and beyond. That pointed to inflation picking up again in the course of next year, putting the inflation target at significant risk in 1998.

13. Looking at the detail, producer input prices remained soft (falling by 2.25 percent over the year to July), and that was contributing to a steady decline in the year-on-year change in output prices (which rose by 2.25 percent over the year to July, compared with 3.25 percent over the year to April, for example). The declining rate of increase in output prices had occurred despite both wage and unit labour cost increases in manufacturing continuing at around 3.5 percent, and despite improving profit margins - at least in manufacturing. The absence of price pressures at the producer level was reflected in recent surveys from both the CIPS and the CBI, and looked set to continue over the next few months.

14. At the retail level, RPIX inflation had remained at 2.8 percent in the year to July, virtually unchanged since January. There had been an unexpectedly sharp rise in service price inflation in July, based on quarterly survey data, which would need to be watched. Even so the Bank still expected RPIX inflation to fall to below 2.5 percent over the coming months as slower producer output price increases fed into retail goods price inflation.

15. Turning to the demand and output data, the Governor noted that the expenditure breakdown of Q2 GDP growth showed that final domestic demand accelerated slightly further in Q2, giving an annualised growth rate of 3.6 percent since the end of last year (compared with +1.6 percent in Q4 and a fall of 0.8 percent in Q3 1995). Net exports had also added modestly to GDP growth in Q2 - though not in H1 as a whole. Output in Q2 had been held back by a sharp downward stock adjustment - particularly in manufacturing stocks which actually fell.

16. Within final domestic demand in Q2, fixed investment rose by 2.1 percent, despite a fall in manufacturing investment; and government consumption grew by 0.7 percent. Private consumption, on the other hand, rose by rather less than might have been expected - also by 0.7 percent, after a rise of 0.9 percent in Q1. Together with the fall in retail sales volumes in July (-0.6 percent after an upwardly revised +1.5 percent in June), this might raise a question about the underlying strength of the consumer demand which was driving the present phase of expansion. But there was a lot of evidence on the other side. In the first two quarters of this year private consumption grew at an average annualised rate of 3.2 percent - significantly above trend and well above the 1.3 percent rate for the last two quarters of 1995. Similarly, smoothed over three months to remove some of the volatility, annual retail sales volume growth in July, at 2.7 percent, was well above the rates of around 2 percent seen at the beginning of the year. The underlying influences on consumption - rising pre-tax income in the personal sector, lower taxation and the various windfalls - all remained in place. The consumer confidence surveys were trending upwards. The July CBI Distributive Trades Survey showed expected sales at their highest level since end-1988 as well as strong reported sales and orders; a very similar picture was reported in the latest CIPS surveys, and in the Bank's Agents' reports. Consumer credit demand was notably stronger in July, rising by 1.5 percent month-on-month and 14.8 percent year-on-year. And there was a continuing steady recovery in the housing market, with prices now some 5.5 percent above their levels of a year ago (on both the Halifax and Nationwide indexes). Taking all the evidence together it would be very surprising if consumer demand did not continue to grow at well above trend - the real question was just how strong would it become.

17. The Governor noted that output growth had been held back by the stock adjustment, which reduced GDP growth by as much as 0.8 percentage points in Q2. Manufacturing output in particular was unchanged between Q1 and Q2, though there was a question about the sharp fall in the sector which includes petrol and nuclear fuels, without which manufacturing output would have risen by 0.3 percent. But here too there was a clear expectation that activity was likely to pick up, reflected in the CBI, CIPS, BCC and IOD surveys.

18. Narrow money growth (notes and coin) had remained strong in July and August - taking the 12-month increase to around 7.5 percent, from the 6 percent rate typical of 1995 and early 1996. Broad money growth, on the other hand slowed in July (+0.5 percent compared with +0.7 percent on average in Q2), bringing the 12-month growth rate down from 9.9 percent in June to 9 percent. The fall in the 12-month rate was affected by the dropping out of the effect on M4 of Lloyds' takeover of C&G in June 1995; and the slower monthly rise in July was affected by substantial overfunding in the month. It was not clear therefore that the slowdown would persist. M4 lending rose by 0.7 percent in July - much the same rate as in the previous three months; and the 12-month growth rate remained close to 9 percent, where it had been since the end of last year.

19. The Governor said that, pulling all this together, there had already been strong monetary growth for over a year. Final domestic demand had been growing quite strongly, led by consumption, for the past six months. And this was now more confidently expected to feed through to output as the stock adjustment worked through. Given the existing slack in the economy, and weak external cost pressures helped by the current relatively firm exchange rate, this was not incompatible with falling year-on-year retail price inflation in the short term. But the inflation target was already at risk, in the Bank's judgment, on an eighteen month view, the degree of risk depending on the pace at which the output gap - whatever that was precisely - now began to close.

20. While the Bank acknowledged that the balance of argument had not changed decisively over the past month, and in particular that the expected pick-up in output had yet to come through into the official data, the Bank continued to see no justification, on the present evidence, for a further easing of policy. In fact the Bank thought that monetary policy would need to be tightened at some point to re-establish a better-than-evens chance of meeting the inflation target. The Bank continued to prefer a marginally tighter policy stance now and repeated the general point that the longer a tightening was delayed the sharper it would eventually need to be.

21. The Chancellor said that the data published in August had confirmed a picture of steady growth. But there were no signs of unsustainably fast growth or of inflationary pressures building up. He was inclined to agree with the Governor that there was no case for moving interest rates in either direction on this occasion.

22. The Chancellor said that the boom in activity that some people had been forecasting did not appear to be materialising. The second quarter figures for GDP growth of 0.4 percent, the same as in the first quarter, had not been revised, although the change in stocks accounted for some of the weakness. Manufacturing production in June was unchanged from a year ago. It was reassuring to see that retail sales were 2.7 percent up on a year earlier in July, although they had actually fallen slightly compared to the previous month. The economy was growing steadily, but it was not eating into the output gap that had accumulated.

23. Recent surveys were more encouraging, and any risk there had been of the economy slowing significantly had diminished. The CBI and CIPS surveys showed a strengthening in activity, but not an unsustainable one. Consumer confidence was also improving (although, as usual, the balance of respondents was negative).

24. The Chancellor said that the price data remained extremely good. Input price inflation was negative and output price inflation at 1.5 percent in July was the lowest since November 1967. Commodity prices, which had been a cause for concern earlier, now seemed to have fallen back. Earnings growth remained constant.

25. The exchange rate had strengthened slightly since the last meeting, representing a modest tightening of monetary conditions. Broad money growth had fallen back within its monitoring range. It had always been suspected that special factors accounted for the rapid rate of M4 growth earlier in the year; and the latest figures were evidence that the factors had indeed been temporary. Narrow money growth, in contrast, had accelerated and a close eye would need to be kept on this.

26. The Chancellor said that increases in house prices were attracting attention, but the evidence showed that price increases were concentrated in particular sections of the market and particular areas where there were shortages in properties. The level of transactions in the housing market remained subdued and the overhang of unsold properties in the market had not been cleared. There was certainly no sign of any housing market boom.
27. In subsequent discussion the following points were made:

-- output had continued to grow in the first half, albeit below trend, despite a significant inventory adjustment. It was likely that strengthening demand that was already evident would increasingly feed through to domestic production;

-- recent data had been largely consistent with the central outlook for the path of recovery in activity anticipated by both Bank and Treasury. By reinforcing that outlook, the risk that the economy might move onto a significantly different path had reduced;

-- while the reduction in producer price pressures had been substantial, this had not yet fed through to the same extent to retail prices. It remained possible that retailers would seek to increase their margins at a time when demand was strengthening. The latest pick-up in service price inflation at the retail level would need to be monitored, although the statistical basis for these figures were less timely than for goods prices.
CONCLUSION

28. Summing up, the Chancellor said that most outside commentators were expecting interest rates to remain unchanged. After reviewing all the evidence, he saw no case for changing interest rates this month, and concluded that they should remain unchanged for the moment.
